# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like: a room full of people who started with different views and ended up aligned, nodding, ready to move forward together. Harmony, in this picture, is the goal. If the meeting ends with everyone agreeing, it worked. If it ends in argument, something went wrong—perhaps the wrong people were invited, or the facilitator lost control.

This picture is comforting, but it is often wrong. Agreement can be a mirage. It can hide the fact that people are uncertain, that they haven't examined their assumptions, or that they're simply being polite. A meeting that ends in unanimous agreement may be a meeting where nobody said what they actually thought. And a decision that everyone nominally supports can collapse the moment it meets reality, because the doubts that were never voiced don't disappear—they just wait.

A better measure of a successful meeting is different: it ends with a precise description of what people disagree about, what evidence would resolve that disagreement, and who will go collect that evidence. In other words, a good meeting doesn't necessarily settle the question. It clarifies the question and sets in motion the work
